title: Who is a true sati
hookLine: not those who burn on the husband's pyre, but those who live in faithfulness (Suhi Var M3, ang 787)

cards: Some words carry a compliment and a wound at once. Sati is one. Around Guru Amar Das, it could name a faithful, virtuous woman.

It could also name a widow who burned on her husband's funeral pyre, a practice found in parts of the society he lived in. A grieving woman could be pushed toward the fire by the very word that honored her.
In the Var of Raga Suhi, Guru Amar Das takes that word and changes who it belongs to.

teach.b: His saloks, paraphrased. One says: they are not called satis who burn themselves with the bodies of the dead. Nanak, they are known as satis who die from the blow of separation.

Another: they too are known as satis who live in modesty and contentment, who serve their Lord and rise each morning to remember Him. He doesn't throw the word away. He keeps it, and takes it off the pyre.
Faithfulness stops being one terrible moment at a funeral and becomes a whole life: modesty, contentment, service, a morning remembered. And the love being measured isn't only love for a husband.

In the language of the Granth, the soul can be the bride, and the Lord the Beloved. So the true sati is anyone, woman or man, whose heart aches at being apart from God and who lives faithfully because of it.
Tradition remembers Guru Amar Das speaking against the burning of widows, and the Sikh Gurus honoring the dignity of women in their sangats.
Today's text is part of that memory, in the Guru's own words: gentle in tone, firm in meaning. And notice who the salok has in view: a woman in grief. The Guru's answer is: live.
Your faithfulness counts in a living life, not in ashes.
If grief ever turns toward hurting yourself, please reach out now: call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

how: Sikhs cite these saloks of Guru Amar Das from the Var of Raga Suhi in katha and in teaching about the Gurus' stand on the dignity of women and widows, and on the Gurus' rejection of widow burning.

games.q: what does “who is a true sati” mean?
o: one who lives faithfully, not one who burns
a widow who follows her husband onto the pyre
a woman who never marries again once widowed

games.q: the salok and the life it describes: tap the pairs.
p: one who burns with the dead
dies of the ache of separation
the soul longing for the Lord

s: Guru Amar Das throws the word sati away entirely
he keeps the word and gives it to those who live faithfully, not those who burn.
in his saloks, a true sati can be known by a faithful life of service
modesty, contentment, serving the Lord and rising to remember Him.
the saloks praise burning on the pyre as the height of devotion
they say those who burn with the dead are not to be called satis.

games.q: a word honors faithful women, and is also used to push grieving widows onto the pyre. you're the Guru. what do you do with the word?
o: keep the word, and give it to the faithful who live.
games.why: Guru Amar Das keeps sati and changes who it belongs to: not those who burn, but those who live in faithfulness.

practice: Hold in mind someone who has lost a husband, a wife or a partner, a grandmother, a neighbor, a friend's mom, and stay with them a while without pity.

Notice what their life still holds, the way they keep going, the people they look after, the small faithful things they do, and let one simple gesture toward them come to mind: a call, a visit, a question about the person they lost.
If you pray, hold them in Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Who is a true sati. Not the one who burns on the pyre, says Guru Amar Das, but the one who lives in modesty, contentment and service, and aches to be near the Lord. Today's word.

orig.note: a faithful woman; Guru Amar Das gives the name to those who live faithfully, not those who burn.

carryVoice: Your line: not the pyre. Faithfulness lives in a whole life, not one moment. Go gently today.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Suhi ki Var, saloks Mahala 3, Ang 787 (satian eh na akhian; those who live in modesty and contentment)
